mcqs.why: Acceleration a = (vf - vi)/t = (30 - 10)/10 = 20/10 = 2 m s-2. Force F = m a = 800 x 2 = 1600 N.

mcqs.q: A 5 g bullet is fired at 300 m s-1 from a 10 kg gun. What is the recoil speed of the gun?
options: 0.15 m s-1 in the opposite direction to the bullet
1.5 m s-1 in the same direction as the bullet
0.015 m s-1 in the same direction
15 m s-1 in the opposite direction
mcqs.why: Bullet mass = 5 g = 0.005 kg. Conservation of momentum: 0 = 0.005 x 300 + 10 x v, so 10v = -1.5 and v = -0.15 m s-1, the minus sign showing recoil opposite to the bullet.

mcqs.q: An astronaut of 70 kg throws a 300 g wrench at 3.5 m s-1. What is his recoil speed?
options: 0.015 m s-1 away from the wrench
15 m s-1 away from the wrench
mcqs.why: Wrench mass = 300 g = 0.300 kg. Conservation of momentum: 0 = 0.300 x 3.5 + 70 x v, so 70v = -1.05 and v = -0.015 m s-1 = -1.5 x 10-2 m s-1, recoiling away from the wrench.

mcqs.q: The recoiling astronaut in the previous example moves at 0.015 m s-1. How far does he travel in 30 minutes?
mcqs.why: Time = 30 minutes = 1800 s. Distance = speed x time = 0.015 x 1800 = 27 m, as worked in the notes.

mcqs.q: A 55 kg cyclist on a 5 kg bicycle starts from rest, applies 90 N for 8 s, then continues at constant speed for another 8 s. What is the total distance travelled?
A 0.4 kg ball is dropped from 1.8 m and rebounds to 0.8 m. What is the magnitude of the impulse applied by the floor?
mcqs.why: Speed before hit: v = sqrt(2gh) = sqrt(2 x 10 x 1.8) = sqrt(36) = 6 m s-1 down. Speed after: v' = sqrt(2 x 10 x 0.8) = sqrt(16) = 4 m s-1 up. Change in velocity = 4 - (-6) = 10 m s-1. Impulse = m x change = 0.4 x 10 = 4 N s, directed upward.

mcqs.q: Two balls, 0.2 kg moving at 20 m s-1 and 0.4 kg moving at 5 m s-1 towards it, collide. After collision the 0.2 kg ball moves at 6 m s-1. What is the velocity of the 0.4 kg ball?
options: 5 m s-1 in its original direction
2 m s-1 in the direction of the 0.2 kg ball
6 m s-1 in its original direction
mcqs.why: Taking the 0.2 kg ball's direction as positive: initial momentum = 0.2 x 20 + 0.4 x (-5) = 4 - 2 = 2 kg m s-1. Final: 0.2 x 6 + 0.4v = 1.2 + 0.4v. Conservation: 1.2 + 0.4v = 2, so 0.4v = 0.8 and v = 2 m s-1, moving with the 0.2 kg ball.

lessons.title: Key Facts
lessons.notes_html:
• When two forces of 4 N and 3 N act simultaneously on a particle, the net force is between 1 N and 7 N. The net force depends on the angle between the two forces. If they act in opposite directions it is 4 - 3 = 1 N; if they act in the same direction it is 4 + 3 = 7 N; at any other angle it lies between these values. So the net force is between 1 N and 7 N. Only if the forces were perpendicular would it be exactly 5 N.
  • A body acted on by forces F1 and F2 producing torque T is completely in equilibrium when sum F = 0 and sum T = 0.
  • If a shopkeeper puts the weights in the pan having the shorter arm of a balance with unequal arms, the customer loses. For balance, weight × short arm = goods × long arm. Since the short arm is smaller than the long arm, the goods weighed are less than the weights shown: goods = weights × (short arm / long arm), which is less than the weights. The customer therefore receives less goods than he pays for, so he loses.
  • A man walking on a tight rope who balances himself by holding a bamboo stick horizontally is an application of the principle of moments.
  • The centre of mass of a body may lie within, outside or on the surface of the body.
  • A cylinder resting on its circular base is in stable equilibrium.

mcqs.q: When two forces of 4 N and 3 N act simultaneously on a particle, between what values must the net force lie?
mcqs.why: The net force depends on the angle between the forces. In opposite directions it is 4 - 3 = 1 N and in the same direction it is 4 + 3 = 7 N, so at any other angle it lies between 1 N and 7 N.

mcqs.q: Two forces of 4 N and 3 N act on a particle in opposite directions. What is the net force?
mcqs.why: When the forces act in opposite directions they subtract: net force = 4 N - 3 N = 1 N, which is the minimum possible net force for these two forces.

mcqs.q: Two forces of 4 N and 3 N act on a particle in the same direction. What is the net force?
mcqs.why: When the forces act in the same direction they add: net force = 4 N + 3 N = 7 N, which is the maximum possible net force for these two forces.

mcqs.q: Two forces of 4 N and 3 N act on a particle at right angles to each other. What is the net force?
mcqs.why: For perpendicular forces the resultant is found by Pythagoras: net force = sqrt(4^2 + 3^2) = sqrt(16 + 9) = sqrt(25) = 5 N, as stated in the notes for the perpendicular case.

mcqs.q: A body acted on by forces F1 and F2 producing torque T is completely in equilibrium when which conditions hold?
options: Sum F is maximum and sum T = 0
mcqs.why: Complete equilibrium requires both conditions together: the vector sum of all forces must be zero and the sum of all torques must also be zero, so the body neither accelerates nor rotates.

mcqs.q: If a shopkeeper puts the weights in the pan having the shorter arm of a balance with unequal arms, what happens to the customer?
mcqs.why: For balance, weight x short arm = goods x long arm, so goods = weights x (short arm / long arm). Since the short arm is smaller, the goods weighed are less than the weights shown and the customer loses.

mcqs.q: For a balance with unequal arms where weights sit on the shorter arm, how do the goods received compare with the weights shown?
options: They are greater than the weights
They are equal to the weights
They are less than the weights
mcqs.why: Goods = weights x (short arm / long arm). Because short arm / long arm is less than one, the goods are less than the weights shown, so the customer receives less than he pays for.

mcqs.q: A man walking on a tight rope who balances himself by holding a bamboo stick horizontally is an application of which principle?
mcqs.why: Balancing on a tight rope by holding a bamboo stick horizontally is given in the notes as an application of the principle of moments, because the moments on the two sides must balance.

mcqs.q: Where may the centre of mass of a body lie?
options: Within, outside or on the surface of the body
Only on the surface of the body
mcqs.why: The notes state that the centre of mass of a body may lie within, outside or on the surface of the body, depending on the shape and distribution of mass of the body.

mcqs.q: A cylinder resting on its circular base is in which type of equilibrium?
mcqs.why: A cylinder resting on its circular base is stated in the notes to be in stable equilibrium, because a small tilt raises its centre and it returns towards its original position.

lessons.title: Short Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Rectangular components of a vector

Rectangular components are the two perpendicular parts into which a vector is resolved, usually along the x-axis and the y-axis. For a vector F making an angle θ with the x-axis, the x-component is Fx = F cos(θ) and the y-component is Fy = F sin(θ). Together they completely replace the original vector: F is the resultant of Fx and Fy.

Line of action of a force

The line of action of a force is the straight line drawn through the point where the force acts, in the direction of the force, extended in both directions. The turning effect of the force about a point depends on the perpendicular distance from that point to this line.

Moment of a force (torque)

The moment, or torque, of a force is the turning effect of the force about a point, equal to the force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action of the force. Proof: let r be the distance from the pivot to the point of application, and let the force F make angle θ with r. The component of F perpendicular to r is F sin(θ). The perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action is r sin(θ). Hence torque T = F × r sin(θ) = r F sin(θ). When the force is perpendicular to r, θ = 90° and T = r F.

A couple: zero resultant force but non-zero torque

This is a couple: two equal and opposite parallel forces acting on a body. Diagram to draw: a horizontal rod with an upward force F at one end and a downward force F at the other end, separated by distance d. The forces cancel, so the resultant force is zero and the rod does not move bodily. But both forces turn the rod in the same rotational direction, so their moments add: total torque = F × d, which is not zero, and the rod rotates.

States of equilibrium: cone, ball and cylinder

(a) The cone standing on its flat base is in stable equilibrium: if tilted slightly, its centre of gravity rises and gravity pulls it back to its original position. (b) The ball balanced on top of a dome is in unstable equilibrium: the slightest displacement lowers its centre of gravity and it rolls away and does not return. (c) The cylinder lying on its side is in neutral equilibrium: rolling it to a new position leaves its centre of gravity at the same height, so it stays wherever it is put.

Dynamic equilibrium: a moving body in equilibrium

A car moving along a straight road at a constant velocity is in equilibrium even though it is moving. Its forces balance (driving force equals friction and air resistance) and its moments balance, so the net force and net torque are both zero. This is dynamic equilibrium: equilibrium does not require rest, only zero net force and zero net torque.

Two principles of stability

The two principles are: (1) keep the centre of gravity as low as possible, and (2) make the base of support as wide as possible. Racing cars are built low and wide for exactly this reason, and balancing toys have a heavy base so that their centre of gravity stays low and within the base.

Centripetal force is perpendicular to velocity

In uniform circular motion the speed of the body stays constant, so the force cannot have any component along the velocity, because such a component would change the speed by doing work. The force can only change the direction of the velocity, and a change of direction with no change of speed is produced by a force perpendicular to the velocity. Hence the centripetal force acts perpendicular to the velocity, towards the centre.

mcqs.q: For a vector F making an angle theta with the x-axis, what is its x-component Fx?
mcqs.why: Rectangular components are the two perpendicular parts along the x-axis and y-axis. For a vector F at angle theta to the x-axis, the x-component is Fx = F cos(theta).

mcqs.q: For a vector F making an angle theta with the x-axis, what is its y-component Fy?
mcqs.why: Rectangular components are the two perpendicular parts along the x-axis and y-axis. For a vector F at angle theta to the x-axis, the y-component is Fy = F sin(theta).

mcqs.q: What is the line of action of a force?
options: The straight line through the point where the force acts, in the direction of the force, extended in both directions
A line perpendicular to the force at its point of application
The path travelled by the body under the force
A line joining the two ends of a couple
mcqs.why: The line of action is the straight line drawn through the point where the force acts, in the direction of the force, extended in both directions. The turning effect depends on the perpendicular distance to this line.

mcqs.q: The moment, or torque, of a force about a point is equal to what?
options: Force divided by the perpendicular distance
Force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action
Force multiplied by the time for which it acts
mcqs.why: Torque is the turning effect of a force about a point and equals the force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from that point to the line of action of the force.

mcqs.q: If a force F acts at distance r from a pivot at angle theta to r, what is the torque, and what is it when theta = 90 degrees?
options: T = r F cos(theta), and T = 0 at 90 degrees
T = r F / sin(theta), and T = r at 90 degrees
T = F / r sin(theta), and T = F at 90 degrees
T = r F sin(theta), and T = r F at 90 degrees
mcqs.why: The perpendicular distance is r sin(theta), so torque T = F x r sin(theta) = r F sin(theta). When the force is perpendicular to r, theta = 90 degrees, sin(theta) = 1 and T = r F.

mcqs.q: Two equal and opposite parallel forces acting on a body form a couple. What are its resultant force and its total torque if the forces are separated by distance d?
options: Resultant force is zero and total torque = F x d
Resultant force is 2F and total torque = 0
Resultant force is zero and total torque = 0
Resultant force is F and total torque = F x d
mcqs.why: In a couple the two equal and opposite forces cancel, so the resultant force is zero and the body does not move bodily. Both forces turn it the same way, so their moments add to a total torque = F x d.

mcqs.q: Which pairing of states of equilibrium is correct?
options: Cone on its flat base: unstable; ball on a dome: stable; cylinder on its side: neutral
Cone on its flat base: stable; ball on a dome: unstable; cylinder on its side: neutral
Cone on its flat base: neutral; ball on a dome: stable; cylinder on its side: unstable
Cone on its flat base: stable; ball on a dome: neutral; cylinder on its side: unstable
mcqs.why: The cone on its flat base is stable because tilting raises its centre of gravity. The ball on a dome is unstable because displacement lowers its centre of gravity. The cylinder on its side is neutral because its centre of gravity stays at the same height.

mcqs.q: A car moving along a straight road at a constant velocity is an example of what?
options: No equilibrium because it is moving
mcqs.why: This is dynamic equilibrium: the driving force equals friction and air resistance and the moments balance, so net force and net torque are both zero even though the car is moving. Equilibrium does not require rest.

mcqs.q: What are the two principles of stability stated in the notes?
options: Keep the centre of gravity as high as possible and make the base narrow
Keep the mass as small as possible and make the base wide
Keep the centre of gravity fixed and make the base heavy only
Keep the centre of gravity as low as possible and make the base of support as wide as possible
mcqs.why: The two principles are: (1) keep the centre of gravity as low as possible, and (2) make the base of support as wide as possible. Racing cars are built low and wide for exactly this reason.

mcqs.q: Why does the centripetal force act perpendicular to the velocity in uniform circular motion?
options: Because the speed stays constant, so the force can only change the direction of the velocity
Because the force must increase the speed of the body
Because the force acts away from the centre of the circle
Because there is no force in circular motion
mcqs.why: The speed stays constant, so the force cannot have any component along the velocity, since that would change the speed by doing work. It can only change the direction, so the centripetal force acts perpendicular to the velocity, towards the centre.

lessons.title: Thinking Deeper
lessons.notes_html:
Centripetal force and the radius of a curve

The car experiences more centripetal force on the curve with the smaller radius. Proof: centripetal force F = m v² / r. Mass m and speed v are the same for both curves, so F is inversely proportional to the radius r. Halving the radius doubles the force. Therefore the tighter curve, with the smaller radius, needs the greater centripetal force to keep the car on the road.

Why a mango falls when the branch is shaken

The mango is held to the branch by its stem, which is strong enough to support its weight at rest. When the branch is shaken, the branch moves suddenly but the mango, by inertia, tends to stay where it was. The stem is jerked and weakened, and the repeated jerks break it, so the mango falls. Shaking therefore uses the mango's inertia to snap the stem that otherwise holds it.

Stability, centre of gravity and toppling

An object topples when the vertical line through its centre of gravity falls outside its base of support. A tall, narrow object has a high centre of gravity, so a small tilt moves that line outside the base and it topples easily, for example a tall bookcase. A low, wide object is stable because its centre of gravity stays above the base even when tilted. Widening the base of support, for example by fitting wider feet or outriggers, keeps the vertical line through the centre of gravity inside the base for larger tilts, so the object becomes more stable and harder to topple.

Why an accelerated body cannot be in equilibrium

Equilibrium requires the net force on a body to be zero, by the first condition of equilibrium. But an accelerated body has a net force acting on it, since F = m a, and a is not zero. A body with a net force cannot satisfy the equilibrium conditions, so it cannot be considered in equilibrium, even if it happens to be momentarily at rest.

Which box tumbles when a truck stops suddenly

The taller box is more likely to tumble over. When the truck stops suddenly, the bottom of each box stops with the truck but the top of each box tends to keep moving forward by inertia. The taller box has a higher centre of gravity, so the forward toppling moment about its front bottom edge is greater and the vertical line through its centre of gravity leaves its base more easily. The shorter box, with its lower centre of gravity, is more stable and more likely to stay standing or merely slide.

mcqs.q: What is the formula for centripetal force for a body of mass m moving at speed v in a circle of radius r?
mcqs.why: The notes give centripetal force as F = m v^2 / r. With mass m and speed v the same, the force is inversely proportional to the radius r of the curve.

mcqs.q: A car takes two curves at the same speed. On which curve does it experience more centripetal force?
options: On the curve with the larger radius
The force is the same on both curves
On the curve with the smaller radius
It depends only on the mass of the car
mcqs.why: From F = m v^2 / r, with m and v the same, F is inversely proportional to r. The tighter curve with the smaller radius therefore needs the greater centripetal force to keep the car on the road.

mcqs.q: If the radius of a curve is halved while mass and speed stay the same, what happens to the centripetal force?
options: It becomes four times as large
mcqs.why: Working: F = m v^2 / r, so F is proportional to 1/r. Replacing r by r/2 gives F_new = m v^2 / (r/2) = 2 x (m v^2 / r) = 2F, so halving the radius doubles the force.

mcqs.q: Why does a mango fall when its branch is shaken?
options: Gravity suddenly increases when the branch moves
By inertia the mango tends to stay where it was, so the stem is jerked and breaks
The shaking makes the mango heavier
The stem becomes stronger and pushes the mango off
mcqs.why: When the branch is shaken it moves suddenly but the mango, by inertia, tends to stay where it was. The stem is jerked and weakened, and the repeated jerks break it, so the mango falls.

mcqs.q: What holds a mango to its branch at rest, according to the notes?
options: Its stem, which is strong enough to support its weight at rest
Friction between the mango and the air
The centripetal force of the branch
A couple acting on the stem
mcqs.why: The mango is held to the branch by its stem, which is strong enough to support its weight at rest. Shaking uses the mango's inertia to snap the stem that otherwise holds it.

mcqs.q: When does an object topple, according to the notes?
options: When its centre of gravity is at its lowest point
When its base of support is widened
When the vertical line through its centre of gravity falls outside its base of support
mcqs.why: An object topples when the vertical line through its centre of gravity falls outside its base of support, because gravity then produces a toppling moment about the edge of the base.

mcqs.q: Why does a tall, narrow object such as a tall bookcase topple easily?
options: It has a low centre of gravity and a wide base
It has a high centre of gravity, so a small tilt moves the line through it outside the base
It has no centre of gravity
Its base of support grows when it is tilted
mcqs.why: A tall, narrow object has a high centre of gravity, so a small tilt moves the vertical line through the centre of gravity outside its base and it topples easily, unlike a low, wide object which is stable.

mcqs.q: How does widening the base of support, for example by fitting wider feet or outriggers, affect stability?
options: It makes the object less stable
It has no effect on stability
It lowers the centre of gravity to zero
It keeps the line through the centre of gravity inside the base for larger tilts, making the object more stable
mcqs.why: Widening the base of support keeps the vertical line through the centre of gravity inside the base for larger tilts, so the object becomes more stable and harder to topple.

mcqs.q: Why can an accelerated body not be in equilibrium?
options: Because equilibrium allows a large net force
Because an accelerated body has a net force F = m a with a not zero, so it fails the first condition of equilibrium
Because accelerated bodies have no mass
mcqs.why: Equilibrium requires the net force to be zero by the first condition of equilibrium. An accelerated body has a net force since F = m a and a is not zero, so it cannot satisfy the equilibrium conditions.

mcqs.q: When a truck stops suddenly, which box is more likely to tumble over, and why?
options: The shorter box, because its centre of gravity is higher
Both boxes are equally likely to tumble
The taller box, because its higher centre of gravity gives a greater toppling moment
Neither box, because inertia does not act on boxes
mcqs.why: The bottom of each box stops with the truck but the top tends to keep moving forward by inertia. The taller box has a higher centre of gravity, so its forward toppling moment is greater and it is more likely to tumble.

lessons.title: Detailed Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Principle of moments

The principle of moments states that if a body is in equilibrium, the sum of the clockwise moments about any point equals the sum of the anticlockwise moments about that point. Example: a see-saw balances when a heavier child sits near the pivot and a lighter child sits farther away, because weight × distance is the same on both sides. If the clockwise moment exceeds the anticlockwise moment, the body rotates in the clockwise direction.

Finding the centre of gravity of an irregular lamina

Hang the lamina freely from a pin through a hole near its edge and let it settle. Hang a plumb line from the same pin and mark the vertical line on the lamina. Repeat by hanging the lamina from a second, different hole and marking the new vertical line. The point where the two lines cross is the centre of gravity, because a freely suspended body always hangs with its centre of gravity vertically below the point of suspension. A third suspension can be used to check the point.

Two conditions of equilibrium

First condition: the vector sum of all forces on the body must be zero, so the body has no linear acceleration and stays at rest or moves uniformly. Second condition: the sum of all torques (moments) about any point must be zero, so the body has no angular acceleration and does not start to rotate. Both conditions must hold together: a couple has zero net force but a non-zero torque, so it fails the second condition and is not in equilibrium.

Improving the stability of an object

Stability is improved by lowering the centre of gravity and by widening the base of support. Examples: racing cars are built low and wide; a table lamp or a laboratory stand has a heavy, broad base; a tightrope walker carries a long pole to widen the effective base and lower the centre of gravity; and a ship carries heavy cargo low in its hold so that it rights itself after rolling.

mcqs.q: What does the principle of moments state for a body in equilibrium?
options: The sum of clockwise moments about any point equals the sum of the anticlockwise moments about that point
The sum of all forces must be maximum about any point
Clockwise moments must be greater than anticlockwise moments
All moments about any point must individually be zero
mcqs.why: The principle of moments states that if a body is in equilibrium, the sum of the clockwise moments about any point equals the sum of the anticlockwise moments about that same point.

mcqs.q: On a see-saw, how can a heavier child balance a lighter child?
options: The heavier child sits farther from the pivot
The heavier child sits near the pivot and the lighter child sits farther away
Both children sit at the same distance from the pivot
The lighter child sits near the pivot
mcqs.why: A see-saw balances when weight x distance is the same on both sides. A heavier child sitting near the pivot can therefore balance a lighter child sitting farther away from the pivot.

mcqs.q: If the clockwise moment on a body exceeds the anticlockwise moment, what happens?
options: The body moves in a straight line only
The body rotates in the clockwise direction
The body rotates in the anticlockwise direction
mcqs.why: If the clockwise moment exceeds the anticlockwise moment, the moments do not balance, so the body rotates in the clockwise direction, the direction of the larger moment.

mcqs.q: To find the centre of gravity of an irregular lamina, what is done first?
options: The lamina is weighed on a balance
The lamina is cut into two equal halves
The lamina is placed flat on a table and its centre is marked
The lamina is hung freely from a pin through a hole near its edge and a plumb line is hung from the same pin
mcqs.why: Hang the lamina freely from a pin through a hole near its edge and let it settle, then hang a plumb line from the same pin and mark the vertical line on the lamina. The process is then repeated from a second hole.

mcqs.q: In the lamina method, where is the centre of gravity found?
options: At the point where the two marked vertical lines cross
At the first hole used for hanging
At the edge nearest to the plumb line
At the midpoint of the lamina's longest side
mcqs.why: After hanging the lamina from a second, different hole and marking the new vertical line, the point where the two lines cross is the centre of gravity. A third suspension can be used to check the point.

mcqs.q: Why does the lamina method work for finding the centre of gravity?
options: Because a freely suspended body always hangs with its centre of gravity vertically below the point of suspension
Because the plumb line attracts the centre of gravity
Because the lamina has a uniform thickness everywhere
Because the pin passes through the centre of gravity
mcqs.why: A freely suspended body always hangs with its centre of gravity vertically below the point of suspension, so each marked plumb line passes through the centre of gravity and their crossing point is the centre of gravity.

mcqs.q: What is the first condition of equilibrium?
options: The sum of all torques about any point must be zero
The vector sum of all forces on the body must be zero
The body must be completely at rest
The clockwise moments must exceed the anticlockwise moments
mcqs.why: The first condition is that the vector sum of all forces on the body must be zero, so the body has no linear acceleration and stays at rest or moves uniformly.

mcqs.q: What is the second condition of equilibrium?
options: The vector sum of all forces must be zero
The body must have no mass
The sum of all torques about any point must be zero
The centre of gravity must be outside the base
mcqs.why: The second condition is that the sum of all torques, or moments, about any point must be zero, so the body has no angular acceleration and does not start to rotate.

mcqs.q: Why is a couple not in equilibrium even though its net force is zero?
options: Because its net force is not zero
Because it fails the first condition of equilibrium
Because it has no torque at all
Because it fails the second condition: it has a non-zero torque
mcqs.why: Both conditions must hold together. A couple has zero net force but a non-zero torque, so it fails the second condition of equilibrium and is not in equilibrium; it causes rotation.

mcqs.q: How is the stability of an object improved, according to the notes?
options: By raising its centre of gravity and narrowing its base
By lowering its centre of gravity and widening its base of support
By increasing its height and reducing its weight
By removing its base of support
mcqs.why: Stability is improved by lowering the centre of gravity and by widening the base of support. Examples are racing cars built low and wide, a lamp with a heavy broad base, and a ship carrying heavy cargo low in its hold.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems — Worked in Full
lessons.notes_html:
Worked Example: Components of a 200 N force at 30°

A force of 200 N acts on a cart at an angle of 30° with the horizontal direction. Find the x and y-components of the force.

Step 1: x-component Fx = F cos(30°) = 200 × 0.866 = 173.2 N.

Step 2: y-component Fy = F sin(30°) = 200 × 0.5 = 100 N.

Worked Example: Unknown weight on a balanced metre rule

Two weights are hanging from a metre rule. If the metre rule is balanced at its centre of gravity (C.G), find the unknown weight w.

Step 1: From the figure, the unknown weight w hangs 40 cm to the left of the C.G, and the 4 N weight hangs 30 cm to the right.

Step 2: By the principle of moments, anticlockwise moment = clockwise moment, so w × 40 = 4 × 30.

Step 3: w = 120/40 = 3 N.

Worked Example: See-saw moments and equilibrium

A see-saw is balanced with two children sitting near either end. Child A weighs 30 kg and sits 2 metres away from the pivot, while child B weighs 40 kg and sits 1.5 metres from the pivot. Calculate the total moment on each side and determine if the see-saw is in equilibrium.

Step 1: Weight of A = 30 × 10 = 300 N; moment of A = 300 × 2 = 600 N m.

Step 2: Weight of B = 40 × 10 = 400 N; moment of B = 400 × 1.5 = 600 N m.

Step 3: The moments are equal (600 N m each side), so the clockwise and anticlockwise moments balance and the see-saw is in equilibrium.

Note: the book prints (60 N), which is the mass × distance product on each side (30 × 2 = 60 and 40 × 1.5 = 60); with weights included the moments are 600 N m on each side, and the conclusion, equilibrium, is the same.

Worked Example: Crowbar lifting a box

A crowbar is used to lift a box. If a downward force of 250 N is applied at the end of the bar, how much weight does the other end bear? The crowbar itself has negligible weight.

Step 1: From the figure, the effort arm is 30 cm and the load arm is 5 cm from the fulcrum.

Step 2: By the principle of moments, load × load arm = effort × effort arm, so W × 5 = 250 × 30.

Step 3: W = 7500/5 = 1500 N.

Worked Example: Force needed to open a nut with a spanner

A 30 cm long spanner is used to open the nut of a car. If the torque required for it is 150 N m, how much force F should be applied on the spanner?

Step 1: Length of spanner = 30 cm = 0.30 m.

Step 2: Torque = force × perpendicular distance, so 150 = F × 0.30.

Step 3: F = 150/0.30 = 500 N.

Worked Example: Tension in the wires supporting a signboard

A signboard is suspended by means of two steel wires. If the weight of the board is 200 N, what is the tension in the strings?

Step 1: The board is symmetric, hung 2 m on each side of its centre, so the two wires share the weight equally.

Step 2: Total upward force = total downward weight, so T1 + T2 = 200 N.

Step 3: By symmetry T1 = T2, so each tension = 200/2 = 100 N.

Worked Example: Balancing a see-saw: where the second girl sits

One girl of 30 kg mass sits 1.6 m from the axis of a see-saw. Another girl of mass 40 kg wants to sit on the other side, so that the see-saw may remain in equilibrium. How far away from the axis may the other girl sit?

Step 1: By the principle of moments, 30 × 1.6 = 40 × d.

Step 2: 48 = 40 d, so d = 48/40 = 1.2 m. Masses are used on both sides, so the factor g cancels.

Worked Example: Tension in two strings supporting a 150 N block

Find the tension in each string, if the block weighs 150 N.

Step 1: Read the figure as a block hung from a junction of two strings, one making 60° with the horizontal and the other horizontal.

Step 2: Vertical equilibrium at the junction: the vertical component of the slanted string balances the weight, so T × sin(60°) = 150 N.

Step 3: T = 150/0.866 = 173.2 N for the slanted string.

Step 4: Horizontal equilibrium: the horizontal string balances the horizontal component, so the horizontal tension = 173.2 × cos(60°) = 173.2 × 0.5 = 86.6 N.

mcqs.q: A force of 200 N acts at an angle of 30 degrees with the horizontal. What is its x-component?
mcqs.why: Working: Fx = F cos(30 degrees) = 200 x 0.866 = 173.2 N. The x-component is the horizontal component of the 200 N force.

mcqs.q: A force of 200 N acts at an angle of 30 degrees with the horizontal. What is its y-component?
mcqs.why: Working: Fy = F sin(30 degrees) = 200 x 0.5 = 100 N. The y-component is the vertical component of the 200 N force.

mcqs.q: An unknown weight w hangs 40 cm to the left of the centre of gravity of a balanced metre rule, and a 4 N weight hangs 30 cm to the right. What is w?
mcqs.why: Working: by the principle of moments, anticlockwise moment = clockwise moment, so w x 40 = 4 x 30 = 120. Therefore w = 120 / 40 = 3 N.

mcqs.q: Child A weighs 30 kg and sits 2 m from the pivot of a see-saw. What is the moment of child A about the pivot? (g = 10 m/s^2)
mcqs.why: Working: weight of A = 30 x 10 = 300 N. Moment of A = weight x distance = 300 x 2 = 600 N m about the pivot of the see-saw.

mcqs.q: A crowbar has an effort arm of 30 cm and a load arm of 5 cm. A downward force of 250 N is applied at the end. How much weight does the other end bear?
mcqs.why: Working: by the principle of moments, load x load arm = effort x effort arm, so W x 5 = 250 x 30 = 7500. Therefore W = 7500 / 5 = 1500 N.

mcqs.q: A 30 cm long spanner is used to open a nut requiring a torque of 150 N m. How much force should be applied?
mcqs.why: Working: length = 30 cm = 0.30 m. Torque = force x perpendicular distance, so 150 = F x 0.30. Therefore F = 150 / 0.30 = 500 N.

mcqs.q: A signboard weighing 200 N is suspended symmetrically by two steel wires. What is the tension in each wire?
mcqs.why: Working: the two wires share the weight equally by symmetry, so T1 + T2 = 200 N with T1 = T2. Each tension = 200 / 2 = 100 N.

mcqs.q: One girl of 30 kg sits 1.6 m from the axis of a see-saw. How far from the axis must a 40 kg girl sit on the other side for equilibrium?
mcqs.why: Working: by the principle of moments, 30 x 1.6 = 40 x d, so 48 = 40 d. Therefore d = 48 / 40 = 1.2 m. Masses are used on both sides, so g cancels.

mcqs.q: A 150 N block hangs from a junction of two strings, one making 60 degrees with the horizontal. What is the tension in the slanted string?
mcqs.why: Working: vertical equilibrium at the junction gives T x sin(60 degrees) = 150 N. Therefore T = 150 / 0.866 = 173.2 N for the slanted string.

mcqs.q: In the same 150 N block arrangement, what is the tension in the horizontal string?
mcqs.why: Working: horizontal equilibrium means the horizontal string balances the horizontal component of the slanted string: tension = 173.2 x cos(60 degrees) = 173.2 x 0.5 = 86.6 N.

lessons.title: Key Facts
lessons.notes_html:
• Work done is maximum when the angle between the force F and the displacement d is 0°.
  • A joule can also be written as kg m² s⁻².
  • The power of a water pump is 2 kW, and the amount of water it can raise in one minute to a height of 5 metres is 2400 litres. The energy supplied in one minute is power × time = 2000 × 60 = 120,000 J. The energy needed to raise mass m through 5 m is m g h = m × 10 × 5 = 50 m, so 50 m = 120,000 and m = 2400 kg. Since 1 kg of water is 1 litre, the pump raises 2400 litres.
  • A bullet of mass 0.05 kg with a speed of 300 m s⁻¹ has a kinetic energy of 2250 J. Kinetic energy = (1/2) m v² = (1/2) × 0.05 × (300)² = (1/2) × 0.05 × 90,000 = 2250 J.
  • If a car doubles its speed, its kinetic energy will be increased to four times.
  • If the magnitude of momentum of an object is doubled, the kinetic energy of the object will increase to four times. Kinetic energy can be written as K.E. = p² / (2 m), where p is momentum. If p doubles while m stays the same, p² becomes four times as large, so the kinetic energy increases to four times.
  • Fossil fuels are not a renewable energy source.

mcqs.q: Work done is maximum when the angle between the force F and the displacement d is:
mcqs.why: The notes state that work done is maximum when the angle between the force F and the displacement d is 0°, that is, when the force acts along the displacement.

mcqs.q: A joule can also be written as:
mcqs.why: The notes state that a joule can also be written as kg m² s⁻², combining the base units for the energy unit.

mcqs.q: A water pump has power 2 kW. How much water can it raise in one minute to a height of 5 m? (g = 10 m s⁻², 1 kg of water = 1 litre)
mcqs.why: Energy supplied = power × time = 2000 × 60 = 120,000 J. Energy needed = m g h = m × 10 × 5 = 50 m. So m = 120,000 / 50 = 2400 kg = 2400 litres.

mcqs.q: A water pump of power 2 kW runs for one minute. How much energy does it supply?
mcqs.why: Energy supplied = power × time = 2000 W × 60 s = 120,000 J. This is the energy the notes use for the pump calculation.

mcqs.q: A bullet of mass 0.05 kg moves with a speed of 300 m s⁻¹. Its kinetic energy is:
If a car doubles its speed, its kinetic energy will become:
mcqs.why: K.E. = (1/2) m v², so kinetic energy varies with v². Doubling v gives (2)² = 4, so the kinetic energy increases to four times.

mcqs.q: If the magnitude of the momentum of an object is doubled, its kinetic energy will:
mcqs.why: K.E. = p² / (2 m). If p doubles while m stays the same, p² becomes (2)² = 4 times as large, so the kinetic energy increases to four times.

mcqs.q: Kinetic energy written in terms of momentum p and mass m is:
mcqs.why: The notes give kinetic energy as K.E. = p² / (2 m), where p is the momentum and m is the mass of the object.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a renewable energy source, according to the notes?
mcqs.why: The notes state directly that fossil fuels are not a renewable energy source, unlike sources that are naturally replenished as fast as they are used.

mcqs.q: In the pump example, the energy needed to raise each kilogram of water through 5 m is: (g = 10 m s⁻²)
mcqs.why: Energy per kilogram = g h = 10 × 5 = 50 J. The notes write this as m g h = m × 10 × 5 = 50 m, so each kilogram needs 50 J.

lessons.title: Short Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Kinetic Energy of a Car and a Motorcycle

Kinetic energy depends on both mass and speed: K.E. = (1/2) m v². A car is far heavier than a motorcycle, so even at a lower speed its large mass can give it more kinetic energy than a light motorcycle moving faster. The mass factor outweighs the speed factor in this comparison.

Comparing the Power of Two Forces

Power = work / time. Power of F1 = 5/10 = 0.5 W. Power of F2 = 3/5 = 0.6 W. F2 delivers the greater power, even though it does less total work, because it does its work in a much shorter time.

Potential Energy Gain on Stairs

Still 4500 J. Gravitational potential energy depends only on weight and on the vertical height gained, P.E. = m g h. The height of the stairs does not change, so the gain in potential energy is the same; running faster only means she gains that energy in a shorter time, that is at a greater power.

Power and Its Unit

Power is the rate of doing work, that is work done per unit time: P = W / t. Its SI unit is the watt (W). One watt is the power when one joule of work is done in one second: 1 W = 1 J s⁻¹. Larger units are the kilowatt (1 kW = 1000 W) and the horsepower.

Renewable and Non-Renewable Energy Sources

Renewable energy sources are naturally replenished as fast as they are used, for example solar energy, wind energy, hydroelectric energy and geothermal energy; they do not run out and generally cause little pollution. Non-renewable energy sources exist in a fixed stock that is used up far faster than nature can replace it, for example coal, oil, natural gas and uranium; once used, they are gone and their use usually produces pollution.

lessons.title: Thinking Deeper
lessons.notes_html:
Kinetic Energy Is Never Negative

No. Kinetic energy is (1/2) m v². Mass m is always positive, and v² is always positive or zero whatever the direction of motion, because squaring removes the sign. The product is therefore never negative; the smallest possible kinetic energy is zero, for a body at rest.

Comparing Kinetic Energies

The first object has the greater kinetic energy. First object: K.E. = (1/2) m v². Second object: K.E. = (1/2) × (2 m) × (v/2)² = (1/2) × 2 m × v²/4 = (1/4) m v². Comparing, (1/2) m v² is double (1/4) m v², so the lighter, faster object has twice the kinetic energy of the heavier, slower one.

Energy Changes When a Ball Breaks a Window

Before impact the ball has kinetic energy. On hitting the pane, that kinetic energy is transformed: part of it breaks the chemical bonds of the glass, part becomes sound energy, part becomes heat energy in the glass and the ball, part becomes kinetic energy of the flying glass pieces, and the ball keeps a little kinetic energy as it rebounds or drops. The total energy stays constant; it is only converted from one form to another.

Work Done on a Boat at Rest

In the physics sense, no work is done on the boat, because work = force × displacement, and the boat's displacement relative to the shore is zero: it stays in one place. The man certainly gets tired, because his muscles expend chemical energy internally, but since the boat does not move, no mechanical work is done on it.

Potential and Kinetic Energy of a Cyclist on Hills

(i) Diagram to draw: two hills side by side, the first taller than the second, with a valley between them; a cyclist path runs down the first hill, across the valley and part-way up the second hill. (ii) Analysis: at the top of the first hill the cyclist has maximum gravitational potential energy and little kinetic energy. Rolling downhill, potential energy converts into kinetic energy, which is maximum at the bottom of the valley. Climbing the second hill, kinetic energy converts back into potential energy, so the cyclist rises until the remaining kinetic energy is used up. Label the first hilltop 'maximum P.E., minimum K.E.', the valley 'maximum K.E., minimum P.E.', and the stopping point on the second hill 'P.E. gained, K.E. zero'. Because of friction, the second hill reached is lower than the first.

Timber as a Renewable Energy Source

Yes, but only conditionally. Timber is renewable if trees are replanted and allowed to regrow at least as fast as they are cut, because the wood is then replaced by nature on a human timescale. If forests are cut faster than they regrow, the supply runs down just like a non-renewable source, and the loss of forest causes other damage. Timber is therefore a renewable source only under sustainable forestry.

lessons.title: Detailed Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Kinetic Energy and How It Is Determined

Kinetic energy is the energy a body has because of its motion. Its SI unit is the joule (J). It is determined by the work done to accelerate the body from rest to its velocity: a constant force F acting over a distance S does work F × S, and using F = m a and v² = 2 a S, this work equals (1/2) m v². So kinetic energy = (1/2) m v², where m is the mass and v is the velocity.

Law of Conservation of Energy

The law of conservation of energy states that energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be changed from one form to another, and the total energy of an isolated system stays constant. Example: a body held at a height has gravitational potential energy m g h and zero kinetic energy. As it falls, its height decreases so its potential energy decreases, while its speed increases so its kinetic energy increases by exactly the same amount. Just before hitting the ground its potential energy is zero and its kinetic energy is m g h. At every point, potential energy + kinetic energy = m g h, a constant.

Efficiency of a Machine

Efficiency is the ratio of the useful work or energy a machine gives out to the total work or energy put into it, expressed as a percentage: percentage efficiency = (useful output energy / total input energy) × 100. There is a limit because no machine is perfect: part of the input energy is always wasted, mainly as heat due to friction between moving parts, and as sound. Since the useful output is always less than the input, efficiency is always less than 100 percent.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems — Worked in Full
lessons.notes_html:
Worked Example: Work Done by an Angled Force

A force of 20 N acting at an angle of 60° to the horizontal is used to pull a box through a distance of 3 m across a floor. The work done is to be found.

Step 1: Work W = F d cos(θ).

Step 2: W = 20 × 3 × cos(60°) = 60 × 0.5 = 30 J.

Worked Example: Power of an Engine Raising Water

An engine raises 100 kg of water through a height of 80 m in 25 s. The power of the engine is to be found.

Step 1: Work done = gain in potential energy = m g h = 100 × 10 × 80 = 80,000 J.

Step 2: Power P = work / time = 80,000 / 25 = 3200 W.

Worked Example: Kinetic Energy After a Force Acts

A body of mass 20 kg is at rest. A 40 N force acts on it for 5 seconds. The kinetic energy of the body at the end of this time is to be found.

Step 1: Acceleration a = F/m = 40/20 = 2 m s⁻².

Step 2: Velocity after 5 s: v = a t = 2 × 5 = 10 m s⁻¹.

Step 3: Kinetic energy = (1/2) m v² = (1/2) × 20 × 100 = 1000 J.

Worked Example: Maximum Height of a Thrown Ball

A 0.14 kg ball is thrown vertically upward with an initial velocity of 35 m s⁻¹. The maximum height reached by the ball is to be found.

Step 1: At maximum height, final velocity vf = 0.

Step 2: Use vf² = vi² - 2 g h, so 0 = (35)² - 2 × 10 × h.

Step 3: 20 h = 1225, so h = 1225/20 = 61.25 m.

Worked Example: Maximum Velocity of a Swing

A girl is swinging on a swing. At the lowest point of her swing, she is 1.2 m from the ground, and at the highest point she is 2.0 m from the ground. Her maximum velocity and where it occurs are to be found.

Step 1: The height difference between the highest and lowest points is 2.0 - 1.2 = 0.8 m.

Step 2: By conservation of energy, the potential energy lost in falling 0.8 m becomes kinetic energy: (1/2) m v² = m g × 0.8.

Step 3: v² = 2 × 10 × 0.8 = 16, so v = 4 m s⁻¹.

Step 4: This maximum velocity occurs at the lowest position, where the kinetic energy is greatest.

Worked Example: Work Done Pushing a Lawn Mower

A person pushes a lawn mower with a force of 50 N making an angle of 45° with the horizontal. The mower is moved through a distance of 20 m. The work done is to be found.

Step 1: Work W = F d cos(θ) = 50 × 20 × cos(45°).

Step 2: cos(45°) = 0.707.

Step 3: W = 1000 × 0.707 = 707 J.

Worked Example: Efficiency of Pushing a Box Up a Ramp

A box of mass 10 kg is pushed up along a ramp 15 m long with a force of 80 N. The box rises up a height of 5 m. The efficiency of the system is to be found.

Step 1: Input work = force × distance along ramp = 80 × 15 = 1200 J.

Step 2: Useful output work = gain in potential energy = m g h = 10 × 10 × 5 = 500 J.

Step 3: Efficiency = (500/1200) × 100 = 41.7 percent.

Worked Example: Power to Push a Box

A force of 600 N acts on a box to push it 5 m in 15 s. The power is to be calculated.

Step 1: Work done = force × distance = 600 × 5 = 3000 J.

Step 2: Power = work / time = 3000/15 = 200 W.

lessons.title: Key Facts
lessons.notes_html:
• When a wire is stretched by a weight, its extension is inversely proportional to its cross-sectional area, and the area is proportional to the square of the diameter. Halving the diameter reduces the area to one-fourth, so the extension becomes four times as large.
  • For wires of the same material stretched by the same load, the extension is proportional to the length divided by the area, and the area is proportional to the diameter squared, so the extension is proportional to length / diameter². The wire of length 4 m, diameter 0.5 mm has by far the largest value of this ratio, so it elongates most.
  • The pressure in a liquid at the same depth is the same whatever the area of the surface it acts on, so for two metal plates of area 2 and 3 square metres placed in a liquid at the same depth, the ratio of the pressures on the two plates is 1:1.
  • The pressure at any point in a liquid is proportional to the density of the liquid, the depth of the point below the surface of the liquid and the acceleration due to gravity — all of these together.
  • Pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted unchanged to every portion of the fluid and walls of containing vessel.
  • The atmosphere exerts a force on a surface equal to atmospheric pressure × area. For a rectangular block of length 50 cm and breadth 40 cm, the area is 0.50 m × 0.40 m = 0.20 m², and at an atmospheric pressure of 100 kPa = 100,000 Pa the force is 100,000 × 0.20 = 20,000 N, that is 20 kN.

lessons.title: Short Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Large Feet of Heavy Animals

Pressure equals force divided by area. An elephant is very heavy, so the force of its weight is huge. A large foot area spreads that weight over a larger area, keeping the pressure on the ground low, so the elephant does not sink deeply into soft ground and its feet are not injured.

Small Feet of Fast-Running Animals

A small foot area gives a high pressure for the same weight, so the hoof presses firmly into the ground and grips it instead of slipping. That grip is what lets a deer push off powerfully and run fast. A small, hard hoof also lifts and moves quickly, which suits fast running.

Pain from Walking on Pebbles

A pebble touches the foot over a very tiny area, so the whole weight of the body presses through that small area and the pressure becomes very large. That large pressure on a small spot of skin is what causes the pain.

Hooke's Law and the Elastic Limit

Hooke's law states that within the elastic limit, the extension of a spring or wire is directly proportional to the stretching force applied to it. No, beyond the elastic limit the object does not remain elastic: it suffers a permanent deformation and does not return to its original length when the force is removed, because its internal structure has been permanently changed.

Force and Pressure

Force is a push or pull acting on a body, measured in newtons (N); it can change motion or shape. Pressure is force per unit area, measured in pascals (Pa = N m⁻²); it describes how concentrated a force is. The same force produces a large pressure on a small area and a small pressure on a large area, which is why a sharp knife cuts while a blunt one does not.

Liquid Pressure and Depth

Liquid pressure increases in direct proportion to depth: P = ρ g h, where ρ is the density of the liquid, g is the acceleration due to gravity and h is the depth below the surface. Doubling the depth doubles the pressure at that point.

Principle of the Mercury Barometer

The atmosphere presses on the mercury in the open reservoir, and that pressure supports the column of mercury in the evacuated tube above it. The height of the column therefore balances the atmospheric pressure: a higher atmospheric pressure supports a taller column. Measuring the column height gives the atmospheric pressure directly.

Principle of Hydraulic Brakes

Pascal's law: pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is transmitted undiminished to every part of the liquid and to the walls of the container. Pressing the brake pedal creates pressure in the brake fluid, and that same pressure acts on the larger pistons at the wheels, producing the large force that presses the brake pads against the discs.

lessons.title: Thinking Deeper
lessons.notes_html:
Springs in Series and Parallel

Single spring: extension x, constant k, since L = k x. (1) Series arrangement: each spring carries the full load L, so each extends by x, and the total extension is x + x = 2x. The effective constant is L / (2x) = k/2. (2) Parallel arrangement: the load is shared equally, so each spring carries L/2 and extends by x/2; the total extension is therefore x/2. The effective constant is L / (x/2) = 2k. In short: series gives extension 2x and constant k/2; parallel gives extension x/2 and constant 2k.

Steel Springs

Steel is more elastic than iron: it has a higher elastic limit and a larger spring constant, so a steel spring stretches under load and returns fully to its original shape, again and again, without taking a permanent set. Iron is softer and more easily deformed permanently, so an iron spring would soon lose its shape and stop working as a spring.

Pressure in a Pool and a Lake

They are exactly equal. Liquid pressure at a point depends only on the density of the liquid, the depth of the point and g: P = ρ g h. The size of the pool or lake, and the total volume of water in it, do not appear in the formula, so at the same depth of 1 m in the same liquid the pressure is the same in both.

Increasing Pressure in a Confined Liquid

By Pascal's law, the increase in pressure is transmitted undiminished to all parts of the confined liquid and to the walls of the container. Everyday examples are the hydraulic brake of a car, where pressing the pedal raises the pressure everywhere in the brake fluid, and a hydraulic car lift, where a small force on a small piston lifts a heavy car on a large piston.

Trapped Air in a Barometer

The trapped air exerts its own downward pressure on top of the mercury column, partly balancing the atmospheric pressure from below. The mercury column therefore does not need to rise as high to balance the atmosphere, so the column is shorter than it should be and the barometer reads a pressure lower than the true atmospheric pressure.

Leak in a Barometer Tube

Air leaks into the supposed vacuum above the mercury, so the space above the column is no longer empty. The leaked air presses down on the mercury and the column falls; if the leak is large the mercury level drops to the reservoir level and the barometer stops working altogether, because it can no longer balance the atmospheric pressure.

Density as a Property of a Material

The statement is correct. Density is mass divided by volume, and for a given material this ratio is the same whatever the size or shape of the object: a small iron nail and a large iron block both have the density of iron, about 7.8 × 10³ kg m⁻³, even though their masses and volumes differ greatly. Mass and volume are properties of the object; density is a property of the material itself.

Estimating the Load of a Structure

The engineer adds up the weights of all the parts: for each part, weight = volume × density × g, using the known densities of steel, concrete, brick and other materials. To this dead load are added the live loads the structure must carry, such as people, furniture, vehicles and wind pressure, plus a safety factor. The total gives the load the foundations and supports must be designed to bear, and it also fixes the pressure the structure exerts on the ground.

mcqs.q: A single spring extends by x under a load L. Two identical such springs are joined in series and carry the same load L. What is the total extension?
mcqs.why: In a series arrangement each spring carries the full load L, so each spring extends by x. The total extension is therefore x + x = 2x.

mcqs.q: For two identical springs of constant k joined in series under a load L, the effective spring constant is:
mcqs.why: In series the total extension is 2x under the load L, so the effective constant is L / (2x). Since for one spring k = L / x, the effective constant is half of that, namely k/2.

mcqs.q: A single spring extends by x under a load L. Two identical such springs are arranged in parallel and share the same load L. What is the total extension?
mcqs.why: In a parallel arrangement the load is shared equally, so each spring carries L/2 and extends by x/2. The total extension of the parallel combination is therefore x/2.

mcqs.q: For two identical springs of constant k arranged in parallel under a load L, the effective spring constant is:
mcqs.why: In parallel the total extension is x/2 under the load L, so the effective constant is L / (x/2) = 2 x (L / x) = 2k, twice the constant of a single spring.

lessons.title: Detailed Notes
lessons.notes_html:
Hooke's Law and Its Applications

Hooke's law states that within the elastic limit, the extension of an elastic body is directly proportional to the force stretching it: F = k x, where k is the spring constant. Three applications: (1) spring balances, which measure weight or force from the extension of a spring; (2) vehicle suspension springs, which absorb shocks by stretching and compressing; (3) bathroom and kitchen weighing scales, which convert the compression of a spring into a weight reading.

Barometer and Manometer

Simple mercury barometer: a glass tube filled with mercury is inverted into a mercury reservoir. The atmosphere presses on the reservoir and supports a mercury column about 76 cm high; the height measures the atmospheric pressure. It is used to measure atmospheric pressure and to forecast weather, since falling pressure often means rain.

Manometer: a U-shaped tube partly filled with a liquid, with one arm connected to a gas supply. The difference in liquid levels in the two arms measures the pressure of the gas above or below atmospheric pressure. It is used to measure gas pressures in laboratories and in gas supply lines.

Pascal's Law and Its Applications

Pascal's law states that pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished to every part of the fluid and to the walls of the container. Applications: (1) hydraulic press and hydraulic lift: a small force on a small piston creates a pressure that acts on a large piston to lift a heavy load; (2) hydraulic brakes: pedal pressure is transmitted through brake fluid to all wheels equally; (3) hydraulic jacks used to lift vehicles for repair.

Factors Affecting Liquid Pressure

The pressure of a liquid at a point depends on three factors: the density of the liquid, the depth of the point below the free surface, and the acceleration due to gravity. It is given by P = ρ g h, and it does not depend on the shape of the container or the total volume of liquid. It is determined either by calculation from ρ, g and h, or by measurement with a pressure gauge or a manometer connected to the container.

Atmospheric Pressure and Its Applications

The atmosphere is a thick layer of air with weight, and that weight presses on everything beneath it. Evidence: a drinking straw works because sucking removes air from the straw and atmospheric pressure pushes the drink up; a rubber suction cup sticks because air is squeezed out and atmospheric pressure holds it; and a mercury barometer column is supported entirely by atmospheric pressure. Applications: drinking through a straw, suction cups and vacuum lifters, the working of a siphon, and filling a fountain pen or a syringe.

mcqs.why: A spring balance measures weight or force from the extension of a spring, using Hooke's law: within the elastic limit the extension is directly proportional to the stretching force, so the extension can be read off as a force or weight.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems — Worked in Full
lessons.notes_html:
Worked Example: Spring constant and weight

A spring is stretched 20 mm by a load of 40 N. The value of the spring constant is to be calculated, and the weight of an object that causes an extension of 16 mm is to be found.

Step 1: Extension x = 20 mm = 0.020 m, force F = 40 N.

Step 2: Spring constant k = F/x = 40/0.020 = 2000 N m⁻¹ = 2 kN m⁻¹.

Step 3: For extension 16 mm = 0.016 m, weight W = k x = 2000 × 0.016 = 32 N.

Worked Example: Density of milk

The mass of 5 litres of milk is 4.5 kg. Its density in SI units is to be found.

Step 1: Volume V = 5 litres = 5 × 10⁻³ m³.

Step 2: Density ρ = mass/volume = 4.5 / (5 × 10⁻³) = 900 kg m⁻³ = 0.9 × 10³ kg m⁻³.

Worked Example: Density of a solid

A solid of mass 60 g is lowered into a measuring cylinder, and the level of water rises from 40 cm³ to 44 cm³. The density of the solid is to be calculated.

Step 1: Volume of solid = rise in water level = 44 − 40 = 4 cm³ = 4 × 10⁻⁶ m³.

Step 2: Mass = 60 g = 0.060 kg.

Step 3: Density = 0.060 / (4 × 10⁻⁶) = 15,000 kg m⁻³ = 15 × 10³ kg m⁻³.

Worked Example: Maximum and minimum pressure of a brick

A brick measures 5 cm × 10 cm × 20 cm and its mass is 5 kg. The maximum and minimum pressure which the brick can exert on a horizontal surface are to be calculated.

Step 1: Weight of brick = 5 × 10 = 50 N.

Step 2: Smallest face area = 5 cm × 10 cm = 0.005 m²; maximum pressure = 50/0.005 = 10,000 Pa = 1 × 10⁴ Pa.

Step 3: Largest face area = 10 cm × 20 cm = 0.02 m²; minimum pressure = 50/0.02 = 2500 Pa = 25 × 10² Pa.

Worked Example: Height of a water barometer

Mercury in a barometer at sea level is replaced by water of density 1000 kg m⁻³, where the density of mercury is 13.6 × 10³ kg m⁻³. The height of the water column is to be found.

Step 1: The same atmospheric pressure supports both columns, so ρ_water × g × h_water = ρ_mercury × g × h_mercury.

Step 2: h_water = h_mercury × (ρ_mercury / ρ_water) = 0.76 × (13.6 × 10³ / 1000) = 0.76 × 13.6 = 10.336 m, about 10.3 m.

Worked Example: Hydraulic brake pressure and force

In the hydraulic brake system of a car, a force of 500 N is exerted normally on a piston of cross-sectional area 5 cm². The pressure transferred to the brake oil and the force on the second piston, of cross-sectional area 20 cm², are to be found.

Step 1: Area A1 = 5 cm² = 5 × 10⁻⁴ m².

Step 2: Pressure P = F/A = 500 / (5 × 10⁻⁴) = 1.0 × 10⁶ N m⁻²; by Pascal's law this pressure is transferred unchanged to the brake oil.

Step 3: Area A2 = 20 cm² = 20 × 10⁻⁴ m².

Step 4: Force on second piston F2 = P × A2 = 1.0 × 10⁶ × 20 × 10⁻⁴ = 2000 N.

Worked Example: Force to lift a car with a hydraulic press

The areas of cross-section of the small and large pistons of a hydraulic press are respectively 10 cm² and 100 cm². The force that should be exerted on the small piston in order to lift a car of weight 4000 N is to be found.

Step 1: By Pascal's law, the pressure is the same on both pistons: F1/A1 = F2/A2.

Step 2: F1 = F2 × (A1/A2) = 4000 × (10/100) = 400 N.

Worked Example: Extra load in a hydraulic press

The pressure in a hydraulic press is increased by an additional 10 N cm⁻². The extra load the output platform will support, if its cross-sectional area is 50 cm², is to be found.

Step 1: Extra force = increase in pressure × area.

Step 2: Extra force = 10 N cm⁻² × 50 cm² = 500 N.

Worked Example: Repeated problem

Problem 6.9 in the book repeats Problem 6.6 above word for word, so the worked solution given there applies here as well.

mcqs.q: A spring is stretched 20 mm by a load of 40 N. What is the spring constant of the spring?
mcqs.why: Extension x = 20 mm = 0.020 m and force F = 40 N. Spring constant k = F / x = 40 / 0.020 = 2000 N m^-1, which is 2 kN m^-1.

mcqs.q: The spring constant of a spring is 2000 N m^-1. What weight causes an extension of 16 mm?
mcqs.why: Extension x = 16 mm = 0.016 m. Weight W = k x = 2000 x 0.016 = 32 N, so an object of weight 32 N produces this extension.

mcqs.q: The mass of 5 litres of milk is 4.5 kg. What is the density of milk in SI units?
mcqs.why: Volume V = 5 litres = 5 x 10^-3 m^3. Density rho = mass / volume = 4.5 / (5 x 10^-3) = 900 kg m^-3, that is 0.9 x 10^3 kg m^-3.

mcqs.q: A solid of mass 60 g is lowered into a measuring cylinder and the water level rises from 40 cm^3 to 44 cm^3. What is the density of the solid?
mcqs.why: Volume of solid = rise in level = 44 - 40 = 4 cm^3 = 4 x 10^-6 m^3. Mass = 60 g = 0.060 kg. Density = 0.060 / (4 x 10^-6) = 15,000 kg m^-3, that is 15 x 10^3 kg m^-3.

mcqs.q: A brick measuring 5 cm x 10 cm x 20 cm has a mass of 5 kg. What is the maximum pressure it can exert on a horizontal surface? (Take g = 10 m s^-2)
mcqs.why: Weight = 5 x 10 = 50 N. Maximum pressure comes from the smallest face: area = 5 cm x 10 cm = 0.005 m^2. Maximum pressure = 50 / 0.005 = 10,000 Pa = 1 x 10^4 Pa.

mcqs.q: A brick measuring 5 cm x 10 cm x 20 cm has a mass of 5 kg. What is the minimum pressure it can exert on a horizontal surface? (Take g = 10 m s^-2)
mcqs.why: Weight = 5 x 10 = 50 N. Minimum pressure comes from the largest face: area = 10 cm x 20 cm = 0.02 m^2. Minimum pressure = 50 / 0.02 = 2,500 Pa = 25 x 10^2 Pa.

mcqs.q: In a barometer at sea level, the mercury column is 0.76 m high. If the mercury (density 13.6 x 10^3 kg m^-3) is replaced by water (density 1000 kg m^-3), what height of water column would the same atmospheric pressure support?
mcqs.why: The same pressure supports both columns, so h_water = h_mercury x (rho_mercury / rho_water) = 0.76 x (13.6 x 10^3 / 1000) = 0.76 x 13.6 = 10.336 m, about 10.3 m.

mcqs.q: In a car's hydraulic brake system, a force of 500 N is exerted normally on a piston of cross-sectional area 5 cm^2. What pressure is transferred to the brake oil?
mcqs.why: Area A1 = 5 cm^2 = 5 x 10^-4 m^2. Pressure P = F / A = 500 / (5 x 10^-4) = 1.0 x 10^6 N m^-2, and by Pascal's law this pressure is transferred unchanged to the brake oil.

mcqs.q: In the same hydraulic brake system, the pressure in the oil is 1.0 x 10^6 N m^-2. What force acts on the second piston, of cross-sectional area 20 cm^2?
The small and large pistons of a hydraulic press have cross-sectional areas of 10 cm^2 and 100 cm^2 respectively. What force on the small piston will lift a car of weight 4000 N?
mcqs.why: By Pascal's law the pressure is the same on both pistons: F1 / A1 = F2 / A2, so F1 = F2 x (A1 / A2) = 4000 x (10 / 100) = 4000 x 0.1 = 400 N.

lessons.title: Key Facts
lessons.notes_html:
• In a solid, the molecules vibrate about their mean positions.
  • The molecules in a gas have random motion.
  • Temperature of a substance is the degree of hotness or coldness.
  • Heat is the energy in transit.
  • In the Kelvin scale, the temperature corresponding to the melting point of ice is 273 K.
  • The temperature which has the same value on the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales is -40°. Let the common value be C = F = T. The conversion is F = (9/5) C + 32. Putting F = C = T gives T = (9/5) T + 32, so T - (9/5) T = 32, giving -(4/5) T = 32 and T = -40. So -40° is the same on both scales.
  • A better choice for a liquid in a liquid-in-glass thermometer is one that will expand linearly.
  • One disadvantage of using alcohol in a liquid-in-glass thermometer is that it wets the glass tube.
  • Water is not used as a thermometric liquid mainly due to its non-linear expansion.
  • A thermometer has a narrow capillary tube so that it gives a large change for a given temperature rise.
